messages.subject: Correcting density with g(0)
parts:
Hi all,


I have a good sized single platform line-transect data set and for a small portion of it I was able to collect double platform data using trackers and a trial configuration. I have calculated g(0) and average p (Pa) from the trial data but I would like to generate density estimates from the full single platform dataset using mcds and correct using the g(0) or Pa in order to use all my data. I am using the mrds packing in R and there doesn't seem to be an option to implement Pa or g(0) when calculating density (using dht function). 


Should I manually re-calculate density by replacing p with Pa in the equation D= n/N in covered area*p? Or Tiago's post on Friday made me think that perhaps I should apply something similar to what he suggested, see below.  There are a few papers that correct densities using the g(0) and I'm sure I'm missing a better way to do this. Any direction would be much appreciated.


From a pragmatic point of view, in Distance you could simply fit a detection function to the data from island B, and then get the probability of detection (P) and the corresponding standard error (se) from the Distance analysis. Then you run an analysis of the data of Island A only, force Distance to use a Uniform detection function with no adjustments, and then add a multiplier that is the P with the corresponding se. In this way, distance will do all the correct calculations for you and the reported results will be the same as if you had used the data from B to get the detection probability and the data from A for the encounter rate, which I believe is what you want (Is the maximum detection distance in both islands about the same?).


Many thanks, 


Gemma

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Correcting density with g(0)
parts:
Gemma


With the scenario you describe, you'll need to live with the assumption that the g(0) you estimated for a portion of your dataset applies to the entire dataset.  To adjust your density estimate derived from the single platform survey, accounting for the g(0)<1, you would do this:


using the estimate of g(0) as what the literature calls a "multiplier".


The harder part of the adjustment is to incorporate the uncertainty in your estimate of g(0) into your adjusted estimate.  If we generically refer to an estimate of a multiplier as "c", then this formula for variance in density comes into play:


where the first term is the encounter rate coefficient of variation, the second term is coefficient of variation for the detection function and the third term is the coefficient of variation for your estimate of g(0).


Multipliers and their use in adjusting estimates, along with properly propagating uncertainty, is described in more detail in Buckland et al. (2001) Section 6.2.3


It is also the case that multipliers have been programmed into the graphical interface version of Distance.  Consult Chapter 8, Conventional distance sampling analysis--section entitled "Multipliers in CDS analysis" for further details.
